title: US Invaded Canada Twice: The 8,891 km Line That Survived Both

minor: 'The USMCA trade pact... faced its first joint review in July 2026, and the outcome is still unresolved.' The review date is sourced, but the outcome is not. The review was in July and the script is dated November 2026, so check the current status before publishing, or say what happened.

'East of there, it runs largely through water': this skips the land sections east of Lake of the Woods (the Minnesota and Maine stretches and the 45th parallel). 'Much of it runs through water' would be safer.
'The Continental Congress, at war with Britain, had written to Quebec's people': the first letter (26 October 1774) came before the war. Only the May 1775 letter was written during it.

'Canada's side answers that much of that gap is crude oil' and 'US officials say the northern border is a transit route' have no sources entry. They are attributed, but the claims themselves are unsourced.
'Both times the armies withdrew': the cold open compresses a long and different story each time. This is acceptable, since the body shows the detail.

shots.vo: Why is it being questioned again now? In 1775, an army marched north to take Quebec.
The line runs from the Atlantic to the Pacific, then up the side of Alaska to the Arctic Ocean.
Of its 8,891 kilometres, 6,416 cross the continent and 2,475 separate Alaska from Yukon and British Columbia.
West of Lake of the Woods, it follows the 49th parallel for more than 2,000 kilometres, a line drawn on paper.
East of there, it runs largely through water: Lakes Superior, Huron, Erie and Ontario, then the St. Lawrence River.
At Detroit, Canada actually lies to the south, with Windsor, Ontario, across a narrow river.
Detroit is the busiest port on the whole border by value of trade, much of it carried by truck over the Ambassador Bridge.

map.label: Busiest border port by trade value (BTS, 2024)

shots.vo: Montreal, Canada's second-largest city, sits only about 50 kilometres in a straight line from New York State.
Today about 41.7 million Canadians live beside about 340 million Americans, a ratio of roughly eight to one.
Even now the line is not finished: Machias Seal Island, in the Gulf of Maine, is claimed by both countries.
Canada has kept lighthouse keepers there since the 1830s, while the United States says the island belongs to Maine.

shots.vo: In the Beaufort Sea, the two sides extend the land border differently, leaving a wedge of sea claimed by both.
In the Arctic, Canada calls the Northwest Passage internal waters, while the United States calls it an international strait.
Yet no national army of either country has crossed this line to fight since 1814, so what changed?

shots.vo: In 1775, Canada was the British Province of Quebec, taken from France only twelve years earlier, in 1763.
The Quebec Act of 1774 had guaranteed its French-speaking Catholics free exercise of their religion and their civil law.

document.title: The Quebec Act, 1774
document.highlight: ...may have, hold, and enjoy, the free Exercise of the Religion of the Church of Rome, subject to the King's Supremacy

shots.vo: The Continental Congress, at war with Britain, had written to Quebec's people inviting them to join.
In September, General Richard Montgomery led an army north up Lake Champlain to Fort Saint-Jean on the Richelieu River.
The fort held out for close to seven weeks, and then Montreal fell to Montgomery without a fight on 13 November.
At the same time, Benedict Arnold led a second force up the Kennebec River, straight through the Maine wilderness.
The route ran about 560 kilometres of bogs, rapids and portages, and it took the men about six weeks.
Counts differ between diarists on the march, but figures of about 1,100 setting out and about 600 arriving are often given.
On 31 December 1775, in a snowstorm, the two forces attacked Quebec City, defended by Governor Guy Carleton.
The attack failed: Montgomery was killed, Arnold was wounded, and more than 400 Americans were taken prisoner.

shots.vo: The Americans kept up a siege through winter, until British ships came up the St. Lawrence in May 1776.
By July 1776 the Americans had withdrawn to Lake Champlain, and the province stayed British.
Even so, the Articles of Confederation let Canada alone join the union without the approval of nine states.

document.title: Articles of Confederation, Article XI (agreed 1777, ratified 1781)
document.highlight: Canada acceding to this confederation, and adjoining in the measures of the United States, shall be admitted into, and entitled to all the advantages of this Union

shots.vo: In 1783 the Treaty of Paris drew the first line, through the Great Lakes to Lake of the Woods.
But British troops kept forts on the American side, including Detroit, until 1796, and the line would be tested again.
On 18 June 1812, the United States declared war on Britain, which was also fighting Napoleon's France in Europe.

headline.text: United States declares war on Britain

shots.vo: President Madison's war message accused Britain of seizing sailors from American ships and blockading American trade.
Britain said it was taking back deserters from its own navy; Madison's message said many of those taken were American citizens.

shots.vo: In the Great Lakes country, Native nations allied around the Shawnee leader Tecumseh said they were defending their own land.
On paper the odds looked lopsided: 7.2 million Americans in 1810, while estimates put British North America at roughly half a million.
On 12 July 1812, General William Hull led an American army across the river from Detroit into Upper Canada.
On 4 August, Thomas Jefferson wrote that taking Canada as far as Quebec would be 'a mere matter of marching'.

quote.text: the acquisition of Canada this year, as far as the neighborhood of Quebec, will be a mere matter of marching

shots.vo: In early August Hull pulled his army back across the river, and on 16 August he surrendered Detroit to Isaac Brock and Tecumseh.
Detroit and most of Michigan Territory passed under British control, and the war's first change to the map ran south, not north.

map.label: British-held: Detroit and most of Michigan Territory

shots.vo: In October, an American crossing of the Niagara River at Queenston Heights was beaten back, and Brock died leading the defence.
The tide turned in 1813: in April, American forces took York, today's Toronto, and burned its parliament buildings.
In September, Oliver Hazard Perry's squadron won Lake Erie, cutting the British supply line to the west.
By early October the Americans had retaken Detroit, and at the Thames River in Upper Canada, Tecumseh was killed.
But Montreal was the prize, since it controlled the St. Lawrence, and two American armies marched on it that autumn.
Both were turned back, at Châteauguay in October and Crysler's Farm in November, by smaller British and Canadian forces.
Then Europe changed the map: Napoleon abdicated in April 1814, and Britain could send veteran troops across the Atlantic.
On 25 July at Lundy's Lane, a long night battle ended with both sides claiming success, and the line stayed on the Niagara River.
In August, British troops burned the Capitol and the President's House in Washington, then withdrew to the coast, leaving the line where it was.
In September, a British army marching south by Lake Champlain turned back after its fleet lost at Plattsburgh.
Offered the North American command, the Duke of Wellington told London it had no right to demand American territory.

quote.text: you have no right, from the state of the war, to demand any concession of territory from America

shots.vo: The Treaty of Ghent, signed on 24 December 1814, returned every captured post and put the line back.
Its ninth article promised Native nations the lands they had held in 1811, a promise historians say went largely unkept.

document.title: Treaty of Ghent, Article IX, 24 December 1814
document.highlight: to restore to such tribes or nations, respectively, all the possessions, rights, and privileges which they may have enjoyed or been entitled to in one thousand eight hundred and eleven

shots.vo: So two invasions, and not one acre changed hands. Why did neither side simply try a third time?
Part of the answer came in 1817, when the Rush-Bagot agreement cut warships on the Great Lakes to almost none.

document.title: Rush–Bagot Agreement, 28–29 April 1817
document.highlight: The naval force to be maintained upon the American lakes by His Majesty and the Government of the United States shall henceforth be confined to the following vessels on each side

shots.vo: Each side could keep one armed ship on Lake Ontario, two on the upper lakes and one on Champlain.
In 1818 they drew the 49th parallel from Lake of the Woods to the Rockies, across open prairie.
Britain still built the Rideau Canal, 202 kilometres long, opened in 1832 as a military route away from the border.
And in 1857 Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as capital, and its distance from the border was among the reasons cited.
The wars were over, but at both ends of the continent, nobody had agreed where the line actually ran.
In Maine, the 1783 treaty's rivers and highlands were vague, and about 31,000 square kilometres were claimed by both sides.
In 1839, lumbermen and state militia faced off in the Aroostook valley, a standoff that ended without a battle.

shots.vo: The Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 split the land, about 18,000 square kilometres to the US and 13,000 to Britain.
Out west, they had shared the Oregon Country since 1818, and a popular US slogan demanded everything up to 54 forty.
In 1846 they split it along the 49th parallel instead, leaving all of Vancouver Island to Britain.
In 1866, Irish-American veterans raided across without US government backing, and withdrew within days.
In 1867, within months, the United States bought Alaska from Russia and Canada became a self-governing confederation.
Alaska cost 7.2 million dollars, and it handed the United States a second long frontier with British territory.

shots.vo: That frontier's last big quarrel, over the Alaska panhandle, went to a tribunal in 1903, which largely backed the US claim.
From 1908 a joint commission has surveyed the line, and a 1925 treaty made it permanent, keeping a six-metre vista cleared.

document.title: Treaty between the United States and Great Britain, 24 February 1925
document.highlight: maintain at all times an effective boundary line

shots.vo: For a century after that, the line was work for surveyors, until a new US administration began talking about it in public.
On 7 January 2025, Donald Trump, then president-elect, said the US should 'get rid of that artificially drawn line'.

quote.text: You get rid of that artificially drawn line, and you take a look at what that looks like

shots.vo: At the same press conference he ruled out military force on Canada, answering in three words: 'No, economic force.'
Through 2025 he repeatedly called Canada a potential 51st state, a phrase Canadian leaders across parties rejected.

US officials say the northern border is a transit route and that tariffs are leverage for tighter controls, and Canada has since named a fentanyl czar and added border spending.

shots.vo: Trump replied, 'Never say never,' and both leaders went on talking about trade rather than borders.
Trade is where the real stakes sit, because a car part can cross this border several times before a vehicle is finished.
The USMCA trade pact, signed by Trump in 2018 and in force since 2020, faced its first joint review in July 2026, and the outcome is still unresolved.
In 1969 the tanker Manhattan sailed through with Canadian permission and escort; in 1985 the Polar Sea went through without asking.

shots.vo: After the Polar Sea row, in 1988 the two agreed to disagree: US icebreakers would seek consent, with neither side's legal claim affected.

shots.vo: So the line itself is not moving, but the pressure on it is, by many analysts' account, rising. What would actually change it?
Start with the outcome both governments say they want: a trade deal, and the map stays exactly as it is.
Then roughly 380 million people keep one tightly linked economy, with goods crossing the line every minute of the day.
Scenario two: tariffs stay, and Canada's government says it will widen its export markets, and its oil already has a route west.
The Trans Mountain pipeline, expanded in May 2024, now carries up to 890,000 barrels a day to the Pacific coast.
From Burnaby, tankers can sail to Asia; before the expansion, almost all Canadian crude exports went to the United States.
Ottawa also points to its EU trade deal of 2017, though the US still buys about three quarters of Canadian exports.
Scenario three is in the Arctic, where more open water could bring more ships into the disputed passage.
There the two already share NORAD, a joint air defence command since 1958, run from Colorado and Winnipeg.
If traffic grows, the question of who controls the passage would move from the law books onto the water.
The treaties of 1818, 1846 and 1908 that fixed the line remain in force, and none of these scenarios needs them rewritten.
So which would you bet on: a deal, a slow drift apart, or a contest over Arctic water?
